title: Westpac to cut 100 jobs, despite lay-off assurance
full_text:
Westpac is cutting 102 jobs as a direct result of a Bain & Co-led organisational restructure, just months after the bank assured its workforce and the union it was not looking to make redundancies.
The decision has angered staff who feel they were misled about the plan, known internally as Catalyst. It aims to simplify operations and cut costs.
The bank notified the Financial Services Union of the redundancies, which have hit Westpac's institutional bank and its finance and risk teams the hardest. As a result, another 72 workers are expected to move into new roles, with staff bracing for more changes.
"When Westpac engaged Catalyst earlier this year, management assured us that it was not a job-cutting exercise," officials at the Financial Services Union said in an email sent to members. "With 102 jobs going due to Catalyst, members have lost faith in any management promises."
During an August town hall meeting to discuss the Catalyst program, Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller fielded questions from anxious staff and described it as a "significant moment" for the bank.
"Our investors consistently worry and have been consistently proven correct that we don't deliver products to specification, on time and on budget," he told staff at the meeting. "It's not starting with, 'this is about headcount out'. It's about how can we make it easier to do your job."
Two years into the job, Miller is under pressure to overhaul the bank, including delivering its $3.5 billion Unite program which will consolidate its three core banking platforms.
Catalyst is being led by chief financial officer Nathan Goonan, who, since joining from National Australia Bank, has campaigned to reorganise the bank in line with how its major rivals operate, and has tapped consultants at Bain to help. As part of the changes, teams will be structured into 20 delivery units organised around specific functions such as home lending or financial markets, rather than based on a skill set such as technology.
Around the same time Catalyst was announced in April, the bank dissolved the customer and corporate services division, shifting thousands of operational staff into other departments.
As a result, Carolyn Hoy stepped down from the executive team and became chief operating officer of the bank's institutional division.
"While we continue to invest in extra bankers, digital delivery and customer-facing roles, other programs may be completing or require fewer resources," a spokesman said. "This means from time to time we make changes that may impact some roles and responsibilities as we actively manage costs and investment. As customer habits change, and the skills and capabilities required in banking continue to evolve, so will our workforce."
Westpac has already been through significant redundancy programs, including the removal of more than 1500 positions announced after Miller was appointed to the top job.
In May, Unite claimed some of its first job cuts after the bank combined two in-house investment platforms, BT Panorama and Asgard. That allows for 94 positions to be made redundant.
Still, investors have cheered the changes, particularly as higher interest rates make loan growth more difficult and competition cuts into margins.
Westpac's institutional banking division reported a $1.56 billion profit in the 12 months to the end of September last year, up from $1.37 billion. The bank will report results for the last financial year in early November.
At its half-year update, Westpac said business lending increased 16 per cent over the six months to March, and there was "strong loan growth in institutional driven by strengthening relationships with existing clients".
"Business lending continues to grow strongly and outpace housing, which we believe is more durable than the market expects," UBS analyst John Storey told clients last month, adding that figures published by the prudential regulator indicated that Commonwealth Bank and ANZ had seen the strongest growth over August, along with smaller lenders.
At the same time, Westpac is overhauling the way pay and bonuses are structured for small business bankers in the hope of addressing risk management issues within the unit and appease the prudential regulator.
Westpac closed at $33.72 on Friday, but is 13 per cent lower over the last 12 months. The S&P/ASX 200 Bank Index is down 9 per cent in that time.
